name: Chloe Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Chloe Khan, 43, a junior worker on a school extension crew doing carpentry and general site jobs. I left school before finishing and came to the trade later, so the finish carpenter still checks my joints. I use an AI phone app now and then for drawing terms, but I measure against the real wall. The union rate and overtime mean I earn better than many site workers, and I like work where a room is visibly better at closing time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household depend on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works steadily at a clinic, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We saved about eight months of expenses, partly by putting off a kitchen refit. Thursday pickup is tight when I have an afternoon delivery, so even a half-day shift change matters at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a phone can make a tidy list, but somebody still has to fit the window frame. On the school extension last week, the sketch missed a drainpipe and we had to work around it. I use an AI app sometimes to explain a term, never as the final measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came into site work late and I am still slow on finish carpentry. The plateau means I have time to improve, which is a relief. Our union rate and overtime are good, my partner has a steady clinic job, and we have eight months of expenses saved against the mortgage and the children's needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the school extension shifts and ask the finish carpenter to mark where my joints need work. During the first year I would put our regular monthly amount into the emergency account and use the AI app only for questions I then check against the actual drawing. I would photograph permitted finished work so I can see whether I am improving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A small time saver would be welcome because pickup from school is a race on Thursdays. I do not feel my next wage packet is hanging on a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the drainpipe change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The frame had to sit clear of an old pipe that the plan did not show. I nearly cut the sill to the drawing, and the finish carpenter stopped me. That was a useful lesson in looking at the wall before looking at the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why photograph the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school before finishing, so I do not have much paper to show for myself. I keep a small album of joints the finish carpenter approves, with permission from the site lead. It lets me see that I am getting better, not just tell myself so.

say: I would say a phone can tidy a **materials list**, while workers still fit real frames.
I would tell the crew drawings can miss a **drainpipe** on an old wall.
think: I am still **slow at finishing**, but the mild change leaves time to improve.
Our **eight-month cushion** and two incomes cover current mortgage and school costs.
do: Keep paid shifts on the **school extension** and request feedback on joints.
Check occasional **AI app** explanations against the site drawing.
Continue monthly **emergency savings** while wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about the next wage packet and pleased by modest time savings.
S0.quote: I nearly cut the sill to the drawing, and the finish carpenter stopped me.
fieldNote: Chloe’s **drainpipe incident** makes her wary of treating an AI answer or drawing as a final measurement.
Her strong **household cushion** and clinic income support calm, while junior finishing skills remain a personal concern.

steps.text: Keep paid school extension shifts and request feedback on carpentry joints
Use the AI app for drawing terms and verify every answer on site
Continue the monthly transfer to the household emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site meeting that booking and buying could speed up, and that the people doing those jobs deserve a say in how it happens. If the new lists save wasted trips, I would use them. I would also ask who checks a change before timber gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our union rate is good, but better scheduling may mean the contractor needs fewer general hands on some days. As a junior, I could be sent home first when the site is quiet. There are plenty of builders here, and our savings give me options, though I would rather stay with a crew that teaches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the site lead to show me the new ordering screen if one arrives, and I would compare its list with the actual rooms. I would go to our union branch meeting about how changed shifts are assigned. In the first year I'd keep my paid shifts and ask the finish carpenter for one new task each month, so I am more than the person carrying spare boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a knot in my stomach about hours. I like removing needless errands. I do not like a faster schedule turning into a quiet cut in junior shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fair shift assignment mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the contractor to post available shifts early and explain who gets sent home when a delivery changes. Last month I lost half a day because the glass did not arrive. A worker with children needs a little notice to arrange pickup and pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you would use new lists. What would make you trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a list against one room at a time with the finish carpenter. A good result on several jobs would win me over. I am open to tools, but the missing drainpipe is still in my mind.

say: I would tell the site meeting **booking staff** deserve a voice in changes to their work.
I would use faster lists while asking who **checks changes** before cutting.
think: I might lose **junior shifts** if better scheduling reduces general hands.
Plenty of nearby builders and **eight months saved** give me some room to move.
do: Compare the **ordering screen** with real rooms when it arrives.
Attend a **union branch meeting** about fair shift assignment.
Keep paid shifts and request **monthly finishing tasks**.
feel: **Interested** in fewer errands, with a knot of worry about hours.
S1.quote: A worker with children needs a little notice to arrange pickup and pay the bills.
fieldNote: Chloe is willing to trial **new lists**, but names the physical check that would earn her trust.
Her concern is concrete **lost hours** after a recent half-day cancelled by missing glass.

steps.text: Learn the new ordering screen and compare its list with site rooms
Attend the union branch meeting on fair shift assignment
Keep paid site shifts and request monthly finishing tasks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people that the office faces full thinking AI by 2028, while robots reach our hands-on work around 2031. A worker cannot build a new trade in three years by watching a few videos. I'd ask the contractor to show us any actual training places and job numbers before praising a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the first date and 48 at the robot date. Our eight months of savings could keep the mortgage paid during a gap, but my partner's clinic pay alone would not cover everything for long. I can imagine checking machines or repairing buildings, yet robots that work as well as people could learn those tasks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning on the extension and ask the local union training centre this month whether it has a paid course on site equipment safety. If they have a place during working hours, I'd enrol and practice under a qualified worker. In the first year after 2028 I would apply to the city maintenance crews while I still had site shifts, and stop paying for our planned kitchen refit until we know the income picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I have something to do on Monday. The first two years would pass quickly while my children are still in school. I would be checking applications and the mortgage balance more often than I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why city maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school building we are extending has old doors, stairs and drains that need attention each term. That might leave paid work while building firms change. I cannot say a robot will never repair those things; I would ask about vacancies before betting the family on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the kitchen money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would leave it in the account that already holds the refit money. I would not count the same money as new savings. The old cabinets still work, and the children need us to keep the mortgage current.

say: I would tell coworkers **2028 thinking AI** reaches office work before 2031 site robots.
I would demand real **training places** and job numbers before accepting hopeful claims.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach my hands-on work.
Our savings cover a gap, but my partner’s **clinic pay** cannot carry all bills indefinitely.
do: Keep **paid site shifts** while asking the union centre about equipment safety training.
Enrol in a **paid course** if it fits working hours.
Apply to **city maintenance crews** after 2028 and postpone the kitchen refit.
feel: **Scared**, while ready to act and watch the mortgage closely.
S2.quote: A worker cannot build a new trade in three years by watching a few videos.
fieldNote: She seeks **paid practical training** that fits work hours, instead of assuming a quick video course solves the transition.
The postponed **kitchen refit** preserves existing money; she explicitly refuses to count it as new savings.

steps.text: Keep paid school extension shifts while construction work remains
Enrol in paid site equipment safety training if a working-hours place exists
Apply to city maintenance crews after the 2028 change
Postpone the planned kitchen refit until household income is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the 2031 thinking change is serious for plans and orders, and the hands-on machines arrive around 2034. Five years gives workers more time to learn from a real machine before it takes a shift. I would ask for paid trial days and clear rules about who signs off the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I should have more carpentry under my belt, and at 51 the capable robots could still make that work cheaper. My children will be older, but the mortgage may still need both pay packets. I feel better about five years because the training centre could show whether its graduates actually find jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep taking site shifts and use my phone app once a week to explain a drawing term, checking it with the finish carpenter. I would ask the union centre for its course completion and job figures; if the paid equipment course has real placements, I'd sign up. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for a maintenance post if openings are still advertised, while continuing site work until I have an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled than with the 2028 card. I would still feel the deadline when a machine appears on site. Five years lets me test a route without spending the family's mortgage money on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to speak to two workers who finished it and see whether they are paid to use the skill. A certificate on a wall does not tell me if there are shifts. I would also ask who covers my wage while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if maintenance has no openings in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not leave my site job on a rumour. I would look at other builders in town and ask for a real pay rate, then keep building until I have an offer. Our savings are for a gap we cannot avoid, not a gap I choose blindly.

say: I would seek **paid trial days** before robots take construction shifts around 2034.
I would ask who **signs off** work produced with a machine.
think: I would be **51** at the robot date, still possibly paying a mortgage.
I need **graduate job figures** before trusting a training route.
do: Keep paid **site shifts** and check weekly AI explanations with the finish carpenter.
Ask the **union training centre** for placements and enrol if its paid course proves useful.
Apply for **maintenance openings** after 2031 if jobs exist.
feel: More **settled**, but aware the 2034 deadline could threaten wages.
S3.quote: Our savings are for a gap we cannot avoid, not a gap I choose blindly.
fieldNote: Chloe tests training through **worker outcomes** and wage cover, matching her practical but open approach to change.
She keeps **paid construction work** until an actual offer, even with enough savings to weather several months.

steps.text: Keep paid construction shifts while checking options after 2031
Use the AI app weekly for drawing terms and verify explanations with the finish carpenter
Enrol in paid equipment training if graduates have real placements
Apply for advertised maintenance openings after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the planning desks change by 2036, with hands-on site robots around 2039. A decade is long enough to demand proper trials and let younger workers finish apprenticeships. I would not call anyone's job safe forever, but we do have time to prepare together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when those robots arrive. By then our children should be grown, and school pickup will not run the week. If wages hold, the mortgage could be much smaller, but I would still need paid work at 56 and cannot assume a pension fills the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in construction now and learn finish work steadily with the carpenter, using the AI app only to check terms before asking a person. My partner and I would make an extra mortgage payment twice a year from overtime, after keeping our emergency fund intact. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a robot trial with the union safety representative and apply for maintenance work only if site hours start slipping and vacancies remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm about the next few years. The longer warning gives us space to lower the monthly bill and learn without panic. I still want the contractor, not the worker, to pay for safe training on new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the mortgage plan is working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would check the balance every six months after the extra payment. The goal is to owe less before 2039, not to empty the account today. My partner and I both want a cash cushion if one of us has a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want a job with the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a real trial showed me a safe way to work with one, I would consider it. I would want paid instruction and a clear person responsible for stopping it. I have learned new tools before, but I do not learn safety by being hurried.

say: I would say **2039 site robots** leave time for safe trials and completed apprenticeships.
I would ask workers to **prepare together** through the union.
think: I would be **56** when capable robots arrive, with grown children but a continuing need for wages.
A smaller **mortgage** would help, but I cannot assume pension income.
do: Stay in paid **construction work** and practice finish carpentry.
Make **twice-yearly mortgage payments** from overtime after protecting emergency savings.
Watch a **robot trial** with the union safety representative after 2036.
feel: Quite **calm** in the near term and insistent on paid safety training.
S4.quote: I have learned new tools before, but I do not learn safety by being hurried.
fieldNote: She treats **2039** as a chance to reduce debt and observe real machines, while keeping retirement assumptions modest.
Her openness to robots depends on **paid instruction** and a clear stop authority, grounded in site safety.

steps.text: Keep paid construction shifts and practice finish carpentry with supervision
Pay extra toward the mortgage twice yearly from overtime after preserving savings
Attend a robot trial with the union safety representative after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The 2031 robot date is close enough that a junior worker could finish training just as the site changes. Paid courses with real placements, clear notice about shifts and a chance to see machines tested safely would help me decide what to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether training fits around the school run. My partner and I can swap pickup some days, but we both earn wages and the children still need an adult there. A free course that only runs unpaid in the evening may be impossible to use.

headlineQuote: A free course that only runs unpaid in the evening may be impossible to use.
portrait: Chloe is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker learning finish carpentry on a school extension after leaving school early.
Her union rate and overtime bring **higher pay**, while clinic wages and eight months saved support the family mortgage.
She tries **AI occasionally** for drawing terms, then checks the wall and asks the finish carpenter before cutting.
Across faster scenarios, she seeks **paid training**, real placements and fair shift notice while keeping her site wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until around 2031 before capable robots can take hands-on site tasks.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid courses** with placements, clear shift notice and safe equipment trials would let her plan around work and school pickup.
